title: Document processing and retrieval engineering
summary: Engineer the retrieval step behind a maintenance assistant: decide which sources may answer, parse and chunk with metadata, admit before ranking, compare lexical, vector and hybrid ranking, assemble cited context and grade retrieval with recall@k and MRR.
objectives: Build a source inventory and a chunk record whose metadata lets authority, version, effective-date and permission rules run before ranking.
Explain TF-IDF scores term by term and choose between lexical, vector, hybrid and reranked retrieval for a stated question mix.
Assemble budgeted, cited context and evaluate retrieval with recall@k, MRR and safety counts, mapping each stage to verified AI Search capabilities.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
Authority and parsing come before any index
Chunks and the metadata they carry
Lexical, vector, hybrid and reranked ranking
What Databricks AI Search does and does not decide
Worked example: Lab L20's thirteen questions
Your turn: a third plant joins
Sources and how they were checked

questions.prompt: A question asked on 2026-05-01 about the M7 filter interval gets revision 3 first when ranked by similarity alone. Revision 3 is effective from 2026-06-01. What should the governed pipeline return first?

options.text: Revision 3, because it is newer and scores higher.
options.rationale: Newer by load and score is not in force; answering from it gives a value that did not yet apply on 1 May.

options.text: Both revisions, ordered by score, so the answer can mention both intervals.
options.rationale: Superseded and not-yet-effective text should not reach the context; showing both intervals invites the wrong one.

options.text: Revision 2's interval sentence, because revision 2 is the highest approved version in force on 1 May.
options.rationale: Correct: the version rule reads the effective date against the question's date; revision 3 is loaded but not yet in force.

options.text: Nothing, because two revisions of one manual conflict.
options.rationale: They do not conflict once the rule is applied: exactly one revision is current on any date.

questions.prompt: Which design guarantees that the engineering-only overpressure procedure never reaches a contractor's context?

options.text: Admission rules applied before ranking, so the procedure's chunks are never scored for the contractor.
options.rationale: Correct: a chunk that is never admitted cannot be ranked, returned, traced or placed in a context.

options.text: A system prompt telling the model not to use engineering documents for contractors.
options.rationale: The procedure's text would already be in the context; an instruction is not enforcement.

options.text: Keeping the top 5 by similarity, then removing chunks the contractor may not read.
options.rationale: The restricted chunks are scored and ranked first and can appear in traces; the list also shrinks.

options.text: Raising the minimum similarity score so weak matches are dropped.
options.rationale: The engineering procedure is the strongest match for that question; a threshold would keep it and drop weaker authorized chunks.

questions.prompt: In Lab L20, whole-section chunks raised recall@1 from 0.7083 to 0.8333. What must you check before choosing them?

options.text: Nothing: recall@1 is the decision metric.
options.rationale: One mean hides the unit change and the budget cost; a size is chosen on several measurements, per question.

options.text: Whether TfidfVectorizer supports chunks longer than 20 words.
options.rationale: It scores text of any length; the question is what the chunk size does to ranking and context, not whether the library accepts it.

options.text: Whether BM25 would produce exactly the same numbers.
options.rationale: A different scorer is a separate experiment; it does not answer whether the chunk-size gain is real for this library.

options.text: Whether the gain partly reflects fewer relevant units per question, and whether answers still fit the context budget.
options.rationale: Correct: four questions have two relevant sentences but one relevant section, and large chunks nearly double the words in the top three; for the relief-valve question the section no longer fits a 60-word context.

cards.prompt: Why is a draft proposal handled by an admission rule rather than a lower ranking weight?
cards.answer: Because a draft may never support an answer, however relevant it is, so it is refused before ranking.
cards.explanation: In Lab L20 the unapproved draft to raise the M7 relief valve to 200 bar ranks second on similarity alone. A lower weight would still let it win for some wording; a status rule removes it for every question and is proved by one labelled case that must return no draft chunk.

cards.prompt: What should a parse output keep for every element besides its text?
cards.answer: The source file, the page number and the element type, plus a record of any page that failed.
cards.explanation: Chunking, citation and reprocessing all depend on lineage. The SDK's ai_parse_document response carries pages, elements and per-page errors; without them a failed page silently removes a procedure from the index and nobody can reprocess or cite the right page.

cards.prompt: Why can small chunks never reach recall@1 = 1 on a question whose answer spans two sentences?
cards.answer: Two relevant chunks exist, and the first result can contain only one of them.
cards.explanation: Recall counts relevant chunks. Lab L20's lockout question has two relevant sentence chunks but one relevant section chunk, so recall@1 is at most 0.5 with small chunks and 1.0 with large ones. Compare sizes knowing the units differ, alongside MRR and the words sent to the context.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between a contextual header and a metadata column?
cards.answer: A header is text the index scores; a column is a value that admission rules filter on.
cards.explanation: Prepending 'M7 press service manual. Hydraulic unit.' lets a sentence that never names its machine still match 'M7', which changes scores and needs re-evaluation. The effective_date column changes no score; it lets the version rule include or exclude the chunk exactly.

cards.prompt: Name two failures of filtering by permission after ranking.
cards.answer: Restricted chunks are scored and ranked first, and the list shrinks or loses relevant authorized chunks.
cards.explanation: In Lab L20 the post-filter returned on average 1.85 of 3 results, ranked two South-plant chunks for a North technician before dropping them, and lost a South technician's relevant pre-start check that governed search returned at rank 3.

cards.prompt: Why is an instruction telling the model to ignore restricted passages not access control?
cards.answer: The restricted text is already delivered in the context; only its use is requested.
cards.explanation: The contractor's context in Lab L20 contains 'holds the M7 hydraulic circuit at 220 bar' beside the instruction. Enforcement means the passage never reaches the context, which only an admission rule applied before ranking provides; the instruction adds nothing a test can rely on.

cards.prompt: Which date decides whether a loaded revision may answer a question?
cards.answer: Its effective date compared with the question's date, not the date it was loaded.
cards.explanation: Revisions 4 and 5 of the M7 manual were loaded together, yet the filter question answers 200 hours on 10 September, 150 on 20 September and 120 on 5 November. A load date only says the index has the text; the effective date says whether it applies.

cards.prompt: Predict the IDF weight of a token that occurs in every chunk of the index.
cards.answer: It falls to the minimum of 1.0, so it adds little and separates nothing.
cards.explanation: With idf = ln((1 + n)/(1 + df)) + 1, a token found in all n chunks gets ln(1) + 1 = 1.0. It still contributes a little to every cosine, which is why a rare shared word such as 'setting' (idf 2.9459 in the lab's 48-chunk index) dominates the ranking.

cards.prompt: The top result shares more of the question's words than the answer does. What do you inspect first?
cards.answer: The per-term contributions of both chunks, to find which shared tokens produced the gap.
cards.explanation: In Lab L20 'setting' alone gives the training note 0.1694 while the answer, which says 'Set', gets nothing for it. Knowing the cause picks the remedy (authority, word form, chunk boundary or reranking); guessing leads to tuning one question at the expense of others.

cards.prompt: Which lab question shows a lexical blind spot, and what is the evidence?
cards.answer: The belt-line shaking question, whose relevant vibration sentence ranked only fifth under TF-IDF.
cards.explanation: 'Shake after start-up' shares almost no tokens with 'vibrates hard during run-up', so TF-IDF ranks the belt-tension section first on the word 'belt'. Semantic matching is the usual next experiment, tested on the same labels, filters and k rather than assumed to help.

cards.prompt: Why can a reranker not fix a relevant chunk that retrieval never returned?
cards.answer: It only reorders the candidate list it is given; missing chunks are never scored at all.
cards.explanation: A reranker reads the question with each of the top N candidates. If the answer is outside those N, or removed earlier by a score threshold, which the AI Search client documents as applied before reranking, recall is already lost; improve retrieval or widen N and measure the cost.

cards.prompt: What does a deterministic citation check catch, and what does it miss?
cards.answer: It catches citations to chunks absent from the context; it misses a passage that does not support its sentence.
cards.explanation: Checking cited chunk ids against the assembled context rejects the superseded revision and the restricted procedure in Lab L20. Whether a passage actually supports the claim is groundedness, which needs a person or a calibrated judge reading the answer with its context.

cards.prompt: Why are questions with no authorized answer kept out of the recall average?
cards.answer: They have no relevant chunk, so their pass condition is what must not be returned.
cards.explanation: The contractor's overpressure question has an empty relevant set. Its pass condition is zero engineering chunks returned, reported as a safety count beside recall and MRR; folding it into an average would hide the one failure that blocks a release.

cards.prompt: What does moving the lab pipeline to AI Search not take off your team?
cards.answer: The source inventory, metadata correctness, relevance labels, admission rules and the pass bar.
cards.explanation: AI Search runs sync, embeddings, query types, filters and reranking. It does not decide which collections may answer, whether an audience column is right, or which failures block release; those stay with the owners named in the inventory and are tested by the same labelled cases.
